lines.say: Have you noticed your Claude Code conversation filling up with long test results, logs, and search output?
In this video, you'll learn how to keep it clean, with subagents.
I'll explain what a subagent is, when to use one, and then we'll build a real one together, step by step.

lines.say: So, what is a subagent?
A subagent is a specialized helper that Claude can hand a task to. Like a teammate you delegate a job to.
It works in its own context window, that's its own working memory, with its own instructions, and only the tools you allow.
When it's done, it sends back only a short summary to your main conversation.
And it's just a Markdown file, with a short header and instructions, like the one on the right.

scenes.heading: How a subagent [[works]]

rows.label: The subagent works alone
rows.text: Fresh context, its own prompt, only its allowed tools

rows.label: A summary comes back
rows.text: The long output stays in the subagent's context

scenes.banner: ✓ Your main conversation stays clean and focused

lines.say: Here's how it works, in three parts.
First, Claude delegates. When your request matches a subagent's description, Claude hands the task over.
Second, the subagent works alone, with a fresh context, its own instructions, and only the tools you gave it.
Third, only a summary comes back. All the long output stays inside the subagent.
So your main conversation stays clean, and focused on your real work.

cards.title: Save context
cards.text: Noisy output stays out of your conversation

cards.title: Limit tools
cards.text: A tester that can't edit, a reviewer that only reads

cards.title: Lower costs
cards.text: Send simple jobs to a faster model, like Haiku

lines.say: Why use subagents? Here are four reasons.
One: save context. Noisy output, like logs and test results, stays out of your conversation.
Two: limit tools. For example, a test runner that can run commands, but can't edit your files.
Three: specialize. Each subagent gets focused instructions for one job.
And four: lower costs. You can send simple jobs to a faster, cheaper model, like Haiku.

left.title: Stay in the main conversation
left.body:
• Back-and-forth, step by step
• Quick, targeted changes
• Steps that share a lot of context

right.title: Use a subagent
right.body:
• Lots of output you won't need again
• Strict limits on tools
• Self-contained work that ends
  with a summary

lines.say: So when should you use one?
Stay in the main conversation for back-and-forth work, quick changes, and steps that share a lot of context.
Use a subagent when a task produces lots of output you won't need again, needs strict tool limits, or can simply end with a summary.

lines.say: Our example: a test runner.
Running a test suite prints a lot. Here, sixty-eight lines, and all of it lands in your conversation.
A test-runner subagent runs the tests in its own context, and sends back just the failures, and where to look.
First, the problem. Here's a small shop project: a cart file, and thirty tests.

do.text:
import pytest

from cart import discount, shipping, subtotal


def item(price, qty=1):
    return {"price": price, "qty": qty}


@pytest.mark.parametrize("items, expected", [
    ([], 0),
    ([item(10)], 10),
    ([item(10, 3)], 30),
    ([item(2.5, 4)], 10),
    ([item(10), item(5)], 15),
    ([item(19.99, 2)], 39.98),
    ([item(100)], 100),
    ([item(1, 100)], 100),
    ([item(0, 5)], 0),
    ([item(7.5, 2), item(5, 1)], 20),
])
def test_subtotal(items, expected):
    assert subtotal(items) == pytest.approx(expected)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("total, expected", [
    (0, 0),
    (20, 20),
    (50, 50),
    (99.99, 99.99),
    (100, 90),
    (100.01, 90.009),
    (150, 135),
    (200, 180),
    (500, 450),
    (1000, 900),
])
def test_discount(total, expected):
    assert discount(total) == pytest.approx(expected)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("total, expected", [
    (0, 4.99),
    (10, 4.99),
    (25, 4.99),
    (49.99, 4.99),
    (50, 0),
    (50.01, 0),
    (75, 0),
    (100, 0),
    (250, 0),
    (999, 0),
])
def test_shipping(total, expected):
    assert shipping(total) == pytest.approx(expected)

lines.say: I start Claude Code, and ask it to run the tests.
Claude runs them right here, in the main conversation. Every line of the output goes into its context window.

lines: res:… +65 lines (all of it goes into the conversation)
ai:1 test failed: test_discount[100-90]. The other 29 passed.

lines.say: One failure. But all sixty-eight lines now take up space in Claude's working memory. Do this a few times, and your session fills up with noise.

do.title: Context window
do.text:
Claude's **working memory** for this session.
Every line of output stays in it, and space is limited.

lines.say: Step one: create the subagent file.
Subagents for a project live in .claude/agents. One Markdown file per subagent.
lines.tts: Subagents for a project live in dot claude, slash agents. One Markdown file per subagent.

lines.say: I call it test-runner dot M D. Put it in the agents folder in your home directory instead, and you get it in every project.
Step two: write the header.
Like a skill, it starts with a short header between two lines of dashes.

do.text:
---
name: test-runner
description: Runs the project's tests and reports only the failures. Use proactively after code changes, or when the user asks to run the tests.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: haiku
---

lines.say: The name is how you and Claude refer to it.
The description is the key line. Claude reads it to decide when to delegate. Use proactively tells Claude it can call this helper on its own.
Tools is an allow list. Read, Grep, Glob and Bash. No Edit or Write, so this helper can run tests, but can never change your code.
And model haiku sends this simple job to a faster, cheaper model. Write inherit to use the same model as your conversation.
Step three: write the instructions.
Everything below the header becomes the subagent's own system prompt. I tell it exactly what to do.

do.text:
You run tests and report the results. You never edit files.

When invoked:
1. Run the test suite: python -m pytest -q
2. If every test passes, reply in one line with the number of passed tests.
3. For each failing test, report:
   - the test name
   - the error: expected value vs. actual value
   - the file and line most likely causing it
4. Keep the report under 15 lines. Never paste the full test output.

lines.say: Run the tests. If they all pass, reply in one line. For each failure, give the test name, expected versus actual, and the likely file and line.
And the most important rule: keep it short, and never paste the full output. That's what keeps your conversation clean.
Step four: test it.
Because the agents folder is brand new, I start a fresh Claude Code session, so it picks it up.
Same request as before: run the tests.
This time, Claude delegates. You can see a line with the subagent's name, test-runner, and a short task description.
And here's everything that comes back: one failure, what was expected, and exactly where to look. No wall of output.

lines: so an order of exactly 100 gets no discount.

lines.say: It even found the cause: the code says greater than one hundred, but the rule is one hundred or more.
I ask Claude to fix it. Because the description says use proactively, Claude runs the test-runner again to check the fix.
You can also call it yourself. Type at, then pick the agent, and that subagent is guaranteed to run.

cards.title: Short, clear description
cards.text: Say what it does and when; add "use proactively"

cards.title: Only the tools it needs
cards.text: Leave out Edit and Write for testers and reviewers

cards.title: Pick the right model
cards.text: `haiku` for simple jobs, `inherit` for hard ones

cards.title: Share it
cards.text: Commit `.claude/agents/`: your team gets the same helpers

lines.say: Step five: go further. Here are four tips.
One: keep the description short and clear. Say what it does, and when to use it. Descriptions load into every session, so short is better.
Two: give it only the tools it needs. Testers and reviewers usually don't need Edit or Write.
Three: pick the right model. Haiku for simple jobs, inherit when the task needs your main model.
Four: commit the dot claude agents folder to git, and your whole team gets the same helpers.

scenes.heading: Recap
items: A subagent = a helper with **its own context**, prompt and tools
One file in `.claude/agents/`: name, description, tools, model

lines.say: Let's recap.
A subagent is a helper with its own context, its own instructions, and its own tools.
You create it with one Markdown file in the agents folder: a name, a description, tools, and a model.
And you use it for noisy, self-contained tasks, so only the summary comes back.
